Benzodiazepines are the first line drugs for SE. Commonly used drugs include lorazepam, diazepam, and midazolam. In children without an IV access, buccal or nasal midazolam or rectal diazepam can be used. Phenytoin as a second line agent is usually indicated when seizure is not controlled after one or more doses of benzodiazepines. If the seizures continue to persist, valproate, phenobarbitone or levetiracetam is indicated. Midazolam infusion is useful in refractory status epilepticus. Thiopentone, propofol or high dose phenobarbitone are considered for treatment of refractory status epilepticus.

First-line therapy involves the use of rescue benzodiazepine in the form of intravenous lorazepam or diazepam, intramuscular or intranasal midazolam and rectal diazepam. Second-line therapies include parenteral levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, valproate and lacosamide, and underlying comorbidities guide the choice of appropriate medication, while third-line therapies may be influenced by the patient's code status as well as the cause and type of SE. The standard of care for convulsive SE is treatment with an intravenous anesthetic, including midazolam, propofol, ketamine and pentobarbital.

Initially benzodiazepines are recommended; lorazepam is the drug of choice. When the SE persists, phenytoin, valproate, levetiracetam, lacosamide, and phenobarbital are administered. The choice depends on the underlying comorbidities. In this phase, only phenytoin is licensed. A generalized tonic-clonic status which is refractory is then treated with anesthetics including midazolam, disoprivan, or thiopental.

Benzodiazepines are considered the first-line therapy during the emergent treatment phase of SE. Antiseizure medicines such as phenytoin, valproic acid, and levetiracetam are recommended during the urgent treatment phase. Midazolam, propofol, pentobarbital, and ketamine are continuous intravenous infusions of anesthetic medications utilized in the refractory SE (RSE) period.

Midazolam, when administered intramuscularly (best evidence), buccally, or nasally, is effective and safe in the pre-hospital setting. The antiepileptic drugs, phenytoin, valproate, levetiracetam and, more recently lacosamide, are used in CSE that persists after first-line treatments (established CSE). Phenytoin is more difficult to administer and is less well tolerated. Evidence of the efficacy of lacosamide is scarce. Anaesthetics are the drugs of choice for the treatment of refractory CSE (not responding to second-line drugs). Midazolam seems to be the best tolerated and is the most often used drug, followed by propofol and thiopental (pentobarbital in the USA). A few studies indicate that ketamine is effective with the possible advantage that it can be co-administered with other anaesthetics, such as midazolam or propofol.

OPINION STATEMENT: Status epilepticus treatment involves the use of several pharmacologic compounds, which are conceptually divided into three successive and additional lines of action. Because of their rapid onset of action, benzodiazepines represent the first approach; these are followed by classic antiepileptic drugs that are administered intravenously. In refractory episodes, pharmacologic coma induction with an appropriate anesthetic is advocated. Apart from first-line compounds, the level of evidence for medications used in status epilepticus is extremely limited. It is important to specifically address etiology in order to maximize the impact of the antiepileptic therapy. The major established drugs used in the management of epilepsy are carbamazepine, valproic acid, phenytoin, phenobarbital, primidone, ethosuximide and benzodiazepine drugs. Carbamazepine and phenytoin are used mainly in the treatment of partial seizures and primarily or secondarily generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Valproic acid is effective against all types of seizures, but it is used most extensively in the management of generalized epilepsies. Ethosuximide is effective against absence seizures. Phenobarbital and primidone are effective against all types of seizures (except for absences) although they are less commonly used because of their sedative properties and adverse effects on cognition. Benzodiazepines are most valuable in the treatment of status epilepticus, but their long-term use is often associated with undesirable sedation and development of tolerance to their antiepileptic effect. Irrespective of the drug used, optimal clinical management requires individualization of dosage and dosing schedules based on careful evaluation of clinical response and sound knowledge of the pharmacokinetics and interaction potential of the individual compounds. Monitoring serum drug concentrations may provide a useful guide to dosage adjustments, particularly in the case of phenytoin, which shows dose-dependent kinetics within the therapeutic dosage range.

Status epilepticus (SE) represents the most severe form of epilepsy. It is one of the most common neurologic emergencies, with an incidence of up to 61 per 100,000 per year and an estimated mortality of 20 %. Clinically, tonic-clonic convulsive SE is divided into four subsequent stages: early, established, refractory, and super-refractory. Pharmacotherapy of status epilepticus, especially of its later stages, represents an "evidence-free zone," due to a lack of high-quality, controlled trials to inform clinical decisions. This comprehensive narrative review focuses on the pharmacotherapy of SE, presented according to the four-staged approach outlined above, and providing pharmacological properties and efficacy/safety data for each antiepileptic drug according to the strength of scientific evidence from the available literature. Data sources included MEDLINE and back-tracking of references in pertinent studies. Intravenous lorazepam or intramuscular midazolam effectively control early SE in approximately 63-73 % of patients. Despite a suboptimal safety profile, intravenous phenytoin or phenobarbital are widely used treatments for established SE; alternatives include valproate, levetiracetam, and lacosamide. Anesthetics are widely used in refractory and super-refractory SE, despite the current lack of trials in this field. Data on alternative treatments in the later stages are limited. Valproate and levetiracetam represent safe and effective alternatives to phenobarbital and phenytoin for treatment of established SE persisting despite first-line treatment with benzodiazepines. To date there are no class I data to support recommendations for most antiepileptic drugs for established, refractory, and super-refractory SE. Limiting the methodologic heterogeneity across studies is required and high-class randomized, controlled trials to inform clinicians about the best treatment in established and refractory status are needed.

Status epilepticus is a medical emergency requiring immediate treatment. General treatment is aimed at restoring physiologic homeostasis, and drug therapy is aimed at arresting the convulsive activity and preventing its recurrence. Concurrent administration of diazepam and either phenytoin or phenobarbital will be effective in most cases. After the status epilepticus has been treated the underlying cause should be investigated and, if possible, treated.

Diazepam, phenytoin and phenobartital are effective in stopping these episodes. Other drugs may be effective in certain individuals, but most appear to work with `hit or miss' effectiveness. Lorazepam has been well established as a first-line therapy. Subsequent steps are less established, and there are many reasonable options, including intravenous fosphenytoin, valproate, midazolam, propofol, and phenobarbital. If intravenous access is not immediately available, rectal diazepam or nasal or buccal midazolam should be given; this can also be used as out-of-hospital treatment to prevent or treat SE. For refractory SE, continuous intravenous midazolam and propofol, separately or in combination, are rapidly effective, with pentobarbital remaining the gold standard for prolonged cases.

Midazolam is effective and safe in the pre-hospital or home setting when administered intramuscularly (best evidence), buccally, or nasally (the latter two possibly faster acting than intramuscular (IM) but with lower levels of evidence). Regular use of home rescue medications such as nasal/buccal midazolam by patients and caregivers for prolonged seizures and seizure clusters may prevent SE, prevent emergency room visits, improve quality of life, and lower health care costs. Traditionally, phenytoin is the preferred second-line agent in treating CSE, but it is limited by hypotension, potential arrhythmias, allergies, drug interactions, and problems from extravasation. Intravenous valproate is an effective and safe alternative to phenytoin. Valproate is loaded intravenously rapidly and more safely than phenytoin, has broad-spectrum efficacy, and fewer acute side effects. Levetiracetam and lacosamide are well tolerated intravenous (IV) AEDs with fewer interactions, allergies, and contraindications, making them potentially attractive as second- or third-line agents in treating CSE. However, data are limited on their efficacy in CSE. Ketamine is probably effective in treating refractory CSE (RCSE), and may warrant earlier use; this requires further study. CSE should be treated aggressively and quickly, with confirmation of treatment success with epileptiform electroencephalographic (EEG), as a transition to non-convulsive status epilepticus is common. Benzodiazepines remain the first-line drugs recommended for prompt termination of seizures. As intravenous lorazepam is not available in France, we suggest clonazepam as the best choice for initial therapy. Rectal diazepam or buccal midazolam remain important options. Intravenous phenytoin/fosphenytoin and phenobarbital are the second-line drugs. Phenytoin is being increasingly substituted by fosphenytoin, but pediatric data are scarce and fosphenytoin is not authorized for use in France below five years old. In children, phenytoin is often preferred to phenobarbital, even though no comparative studies have demonstrated a better efficacy. To manage status epilepticus refractory to a benzodiazepine and administration of phenytoin and/or phenobarbital, many pediatricians today prefer high-dose midazolam infusion rather than thiopental to minimize serious side effects from barbiturate anesthesia.

The MitraClip (Abbott Vascular, Menlo Park, CA) is a device used to perform transcatheter edge-to-edge repair of the mitral valve approved by the Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of high-risk degenerative mitral regurgitation.
The MitraClip device is a percutaneous catheter-delivered, implantable clip that reduces mitral regurgitation by approximating the edges of the mitral leaflets, creating an "edge-to-edge" repair.
The MitraClip (Abbot Vascular) is a medical device that is percutaneously implanted and designed to eliminate leaking of the mitral valve.
The MitraClip system can be used to control regurgitant blood flow in patients with mitral regurgitation who cannot tolerate open surgery to replace the mitral valve.

questions.body: Which modifications protect mRNAs from degradation by cytoplasmic RNases?
ideal_answer: mRNAs are synthesized through transcription in the cell nucleus, using DNA as a template. Following transcription, eukaryotic mRNAs undergo a series of processing steps collectively known as mRNA maturation. During this process, introns are removed through splicing, and exons are joined together to form a continuous coding sequence. However, even after splicing, mRNAs are not yet fully competent for export to the cytoplasm or for efficient translation. Additional modifications are required to enhance their stability and protect them from degradation by cytoplasmic RNases. The main protective modifications include four key features: (1) the addition of a 5′ cap structure, (2) polyadenylation of the 3′ end, (3) the association with RNA-binding proteins that interact directly or indirectly with these terminal modifications, and (4) internal chemical modifications, collectively referred to as epitranscriptomic modifications, which contribute to mRNA stability and regulation. These structural and chemical modifications protect mRNAs from exonucleolytic degradation, facilitate nuclear export, and enhance translational efficiency. Overall, they play a crucial role in extending mRNA lifespan and ensuring proper gene expression by reducing susceptibility to RNase-mediated degradation.

Messenger RNAs are protected from degradation by cytoplasmic RNases through several modifications: the 5' N7-methylguanosine cap (including Cap1 structures), which is critical for mRNA stability and can be actively restored; the 3' poly(A) tail, which binds poly(A)-binding proteins (PABPs) to form a stabilizing closed-loop messenger ribonucleoprotein (mRNP) structure; and internal nucleotide modifications, such as N6-methyladenosine (m6A), which enhance stability by acting as physical barriers or directing RNA structural rearrangements.

Studies have shown that modifications such as 5'-N 7-methylated guanosine triphosphate cap structure and 3' poly(A) tail play a crucial role in protecting mRNAs from degradation by cytoplasmic RNases. Addition of these structures increases mRNA stability, with 5' capping structure and 3' poly A tail preventing degradation by nucleases. Furthermore, nanoparticle delivery system also protects mRNA from degradation by ubiquitous nucleases, enhancing mRNA concentration in circulation and assisting its cytoplasmic entrance. Polyadenylation adds a 3' poly(A) tail, providing a binding site for poly(A)-binding proteins (PABPs), which regulate mRNA stability and translation initiation. Additionally, N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification has been found to modulate translational dynamics, potentially influencing mRNA stability by recruiting translation machinery proteins or directing RNA structural rearrangement. These modifications work together to ensure mRNA stability and prevent degradation, making them essential for effective mRNA translation and function.

The primary modifications that protect mRNAs from degradation by cytoplasmic RNases are the 5' 7-methylguanosine cap and the 3' poly(A) tail. The 5' cap structure is essential for limiting degradation by cellular 5'-3' exonucleases. The 3' poly(A) tail, typically associated with poly(A)-binding proteins (PABPs), shields the transcript from deadenylases and 3'-5' exonucleases. In some transcripts, highly conserved triple helical structures or 3' histone stem-loop elements provide stability in place of or in addition to a poly(A) tail. Epitranscriptomic modifications, such as N6-methyladenosine (m6A), and the incorporation of specific residues like 2'OMeU also influence mRNA dynamics and enhance resistance to degradation. Furthermore, regulatory proteins including LARP1, LARP4, and insulin-like growth factor 2 mRNA-binding proteins (IGF2BPs) contribute to mRNA stability by protecting the poly(A) tail or maintaining the integrity of the transcript against nucleolytic attack.

The primary modifications that protect mRNAs from degradation by cytoplasmic RNases are:

1. **5' Cap Structure**: The N7-methylguanosine cap at the 5' end shields the mRNA from exonucleases and enhances stability.

2. **3' Poly-A Tail**: This tail, along with poly(A)-binding proteins (PABPs), protects the mRNA from degradation and aids in translation by forming a closed loop structure.

3. **m6A Modifications**: These epitranscriptomic marks influence RNA stability and translation by recruiting proteins or altering RNA structure, adding another layer of protection.

These modifications collectively enhance mRNA stability and facilitate efficient translation in the cytoplasm.

mRNAs are protected from degradation and stabilized by modifications such as the 5´ capping structure (including the N7-methylguanosine cap and Cap 1 structure) and the 3´ poly(A) tail. Additionally, association with PABP, the epitranscriptomic modification N6-methyladenosine (m6A), and the use of nanoparticle delivery systems help protect mRNA from ubiquitous nucleases and enhance stability.

Modifications that protect mRNAs from degradation by cytoplasmic RNases include the 5'-N7-methylated guanosine triphosphate cap structure and the 3' poly(A) tail. The 5' cap, added in the nucleus, plays a critical role in mRNA translation and stability, while the 3' poly(A) tail provides a binding site for poly(A)-binding proteins (PABPs) that regulate mRNA stability and translation. Additionally, the N6-methyladenosine (m6A) epitranscriptomic code has been found to modulate translational dynamics and protect mRNAs from degradation. These modifications work together to enhance mRNA stability and translation efficiency.

Eukaryotic mRNAs are protected from degradation by cytoplasmic RNases through several key modifications and mechanisms. The primary modifications include the addition of an N7-methylguanosine (m7G) cap at the 5' end and a poly(A) tail at the 3' end. The 5' cap protects the transcript from 5'-3' exoribonucleases, while the 3' poly(A) tail, particularly when bound by poly(A)-binding proteins (PABPs), enhances stability and promotes the formation of a protective closed-loop structure. Internal epitranscriptomic modifications, such as N6-methyladenosine (m6A), also contribute to mRNA stability. Furthermore, physical mechanisms provide protection, such as the occupancy of mRNA by ribosomes, which can hinder RNase access to the transcript. Additionally, the sequestration of mRNAs into ribonucleoprotein complexes, such as stress granules and processing bodies (PBs), can shield them from degradation during physiological stress or starvation.

mRNA stability, which protects against degradation by cytoplasmic RNases, is enhanced by several intrinsic modifications. These include the 5' capping structure, which plays a critical role in mRNA stability; the 3' poly(A) tail, which increases mRNA stability and facilitates the formation of a protective 'closed loop' structure via Poly(A)-binding proteins (PABPs); and the epitranscriptomic modification N6-methyladenosine (m6A), which is crucial for mediating translatomic stability and can act as a physical barrier.

The modifications that protect mRNAs from degradation by cytoplasmic RNases are the 5' cap (including its N7-methylguanosine form), the 3' poly(A) tail stabilized by poly(A)-binding proteins, and the N6-methyladenosine (m6A) epitranscriptomic mark.

The main protective modifications are the 5′ cap and the 3′ poly(A) tail. In eukaryotic mRNAs, the 5′ N7-methylguanosine cap, especially when properly methylated, protects the transcript from decapping and cytoplasmic degradation, while the 3′ poly(A) tail, together with poly(A)-binding proteins, shields the RNA from exonucleases. Additional cap-associated methylations such as m6Am and 2′-O-methylation can further increase stability by making mRNAs more resistant to decapping and degradation.

Modifications that protect cytoplasmic mRNAs from RNases include the 5' cap (with cap-1/cap-2 2'-O-methylation), the 3' poly(A) tail bound by PABPC, and internal base modifications such as pseudouridine, N1-methylpseudouridine, and N6-methyladenosine. RNA-binding proteins like PABPC1 and ELAVL1/HuR mask mRNAs and protect them from cytoplasmic exoribonucleases.

Messenger RNAs are protected from degradation by several key modifications and structural elements. The 5' 7-methylguanosine cap is essential for limiting degradation by cellular 5'-3' exonucleases. At the 3' end, the poly(A) tail protects the transcript from 3'-5' exonucleases, a process often mediated by its interaction with poly(A)-binding proteins (PABPs) and proteins like LARP1 and LARP4. In transcripts lacking a poly(A) tail, stability can be provided by 3' histone stem-loop elements or highly conserved triple helical RNA structures that shield the mRNA from deadenylation and decay. Additionally, internal chemical modifications such as N6-methyladenosine (m6A) can influence stability, particularly when recognized by readers like IGF2BPs that maintain mRNA integrity. The incorporation of specific residues, such as 2'OMeU, has also been shown to enhance resistance to cellular exonucleases.

Cytoplasmic mRNAs are protected from degradation by RNases through several chemical and structural features. Nucleoside sugar modifications such as 2′-O-methyl (2′-O-Me) and 2′-fluoro (2′-F) increase resistance to enzymatic degradation in RNase-rich environments. In eukaryotes, 5′-end cap structure modifications are key determinants of mRNA stability, and the presence of a 5′ cap itself protects mRNAs from nuclease attack; fully processed cytoplasmic mRNAs also carry a 3′ poly(A) tail, which contributes to stability. Additionally, stable terminal hairpin structures at mRNA ends can protect transcripts from poly(A)-dependent ribonucleases. Finally, antisense RNA–mRNA duplex formation can mask RNase recognition sites (e.g., for RNase E), increasing mRNA stability.

mRNAs are protected from cytoplasmic RNase degradation through several key modifications and mechanisms. The 5' cap structure, a specially modified nucleotide at the 5' end, protects against 5' to 3' exonuclease activity. The 3' poly(A) tail, consisting of multiple adenosine monophosphates at the 3' end, protects against 3' to 5' exonuclease degradation. Chemical modifications such as pseudouridine, 2'-O-methylation, and N6-methyladenosine (m6A) enhance RNA stability and influence mRNA localization. Protein-mediated protection includes RNA-binding proteins like PABP and HuR/ELAVL1, as well as ribonucleoprotein complexes that shield mRNA from degradation machinery. Stress granules are cytoplasmic compartments that sequester and protect mRNAs during cellular stress. These modifications and mechanisms work together, with the 5' cap and 3' poly(A) tail forming the primary structural defense, while chemical modifications and protein binding provide additional layers of protection against cytoplasmic RNases such as XRN1, DCP2, and the exosome complex.

mRNAs are protected from cytoplasmic RNase-mediated degradation by both terminal and internal chemical modifications. At the 5′ end, the N7‑methylguanosine (m7G) cap (including cap variants with ribose 2′‑O‑methylation; cap 1/cap 2) protects transcripts from exonucleolytic decay. At the 3′ end, the poly(A) tail, together with its poly(A)-binding protein, helps shield polyadenylated mRNAs from indiscriminate nuclease attack. In addition, chemical modification of the ribose 2′‑OH (e.g., widespread 2′‑O‑methylation) and nucleotide analog substitutions such as 2′‑O‑Me and 2′‑F increase resistance to enzymatic degradation and stabilize mRNA in RNase-rich environments.

The primary modifications that protect mRNAs from degradation by cytoplasmic RNases are the 5' N7-methylguanosine (m7G) cap (including cap-0 and cap-1 structures), the 3' poly(A) tail, and chemical modifications of the poly(A) tail such as phosphorothioate, 2'-O-methyl, and 2'-O-methoxyethyl substitutions. The 5' cap protects against 5' exonucleases (e.g., Xrn1) and decapping enzymes (e.g., DCP2), while the poly(A) tail and its chemical modifications inhibit 3' deadenylation (e.g., resistance to CAF1) and enhance stability, often by retaining poly(A)-binding protein (PABP) interactions. Additionally, m6Am (N6,2'-O-dimethyladenosine) at the 5' cap-adjacent nucleotide confers resistance to DCP2 decapping, and 2'-O-methyl/2'-fluoro ribose modifications protect synthetic mRNAs from enzymatic degradation in RNase-rich environments.

ideal_answer: Super-enhancers (SEs) consist of clusters of enhancers that are enriched at high density with transcription factors, histone-modifying enzymes and cofactors. Therefore, super-enhancers differ from typical enhancers in size, transcription factor density and content, ability to activate transcription, and sensitivity to perturbation. Because of their characteristics, they have been shown to play an important role in the control of cell identity and tumorigenesis.

Super-enhancers (SEs) differ from typical enhancers in several key aspects: they are larger, consist of clusters of multiple typical enhancers, and form unusual enhancer domains. SEs exhibit a significantly higher local density and content of transcription factors, including cell-type-specific master regulators (e.g., Oct4, Sox2, Nanog), Mediator, histone-modifying enzymes, and cofactors. This enriched molecular composition contributes to their greater ability to activate transcription, particularly for genes crucial for establishing and maintaining cell identity. Furthermore, SEs demonstrate increased sensitivity to perturbation; reductions in master transcription factor or Mediator levels cause a preferential loss of expression of SE-associated genes compared to other genes. In pathological contexts, oncogenic SEs play a significant role in promoting tumorigenesis and malignancy by altering gene expression, making them potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

questions.body: Is alcoholism considered a treatable disease?
ideal_answer: Until recently, alcoholism was widely regarded as an incurable psychological disorder. However, over the past decade, a growing body of research has provided new insights into the underlying causes of alcohol craving and its potential treatment. The brain contains receptor sites for naturally occurring opioid-like substances, such as endorphins and enkephalins, which are produced by the nervous system. Exogenous opiates, including morphine and heroin, as well as certain metabolic byproducts of alcohol, can also bind to these receptors. Alcohol craving has been associated with deficiencies in these endogenous opioid-like substances, as well as in other neurotransmitter systems. Such deficiencies may arise due to genetic predisposition, prolonged stress, or chronic heavy alcohol consumption. This neurochemical imbalance can, in some cases, be addressed pharmacologically, potentially reducing alcohol craving - particularly when combined with psychotherapeutic and counseling interventions. For instance, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, initially developed for the treatment of obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus, have recently shown promise in the treatment of substance use disorders (SUDs), including alcohol use disorder (AUD). Preclinical studies in rodents and non-human primates have demonstrated that GLP-1 analogs can reduce substance intake, including alcohol and nicotine, likely through modulation of neurotransmitter systems involved in reward and reinforcement. Additionally, these agents may exert neuroprotective effects by reducing oxidative stress and neuroinflammation associated with chronic substance use. Beyond pharmacological approaches, virtual reality (VR) technology has emerged as a novel therapeutic tool. In the context of AUD, VR can be applied in various settings, including exposure therapy, diagnostic assessment, and interactive behavioral interventions. However, as a relatively recent development, VR-based therapies require further research to establish their efficacy, safety, and long-term applicability. In summary, alcoholism is now recognized as a treatable condition, with a range of therapeutic options spanning conventional pharmacological treatments to emerging non-pharmacological approaches.

GSCs contribute to tumor heterogeneity and recapitulate pathway alterations described for the different GBM subtypes found in patients. Evidence from mouse models indicates that GSCs repopulate brain tumors after therapeutic intervention, and due to GSC plasticity, they reconstitute heterogeneity in recurrent tumors. Angiomyolipoma (AML) is a benign mesenchymal tumor composed of blood vessels, smooth muscle, and adipose tissue, often classified as a PEComa. Angiomyolipoma (AML) is a mesenchymal neoplasm belonging to the perivascular epithelioid cell (PEComa) family, characterized by its composition of smooth muscle cells, blood vessels, and adipose tissue. While most commonly found in the kidney, AML can also occur in extrarenal sites such as the liver and mucocutaneous areas like the nasal cavity and skin. Typical renal AMLs are generally benign and often easily diagnosed by the presence of adipose tissue on imaging. However, fat-poor AMLs, which lack significant adipose tissue, can mimic malignant tumors like cystic renal cell carcinoma, requiring histopathological examination that may reveal necrosis, hematoma, and scant adipose/muscle tissue for definitive diagnosis. Hepatic AML is often an incidental finding, and while fat components and early venous return on CT angiography can be diagnostic clues, diffusion-weighted MRI apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) values may overlap with other benign and malignant liver tumors, limiting specificity. A crucial distinction is made between mucocutaneous AML, which is typically benign, and hepatorenal AML, which may possess malignant potential, highlighting the importance of subtype and location in assessing prognosis. In cases of atypical presentation, fat-poor lesions, or extrarenal locations, histopathological confirmation through biopsy or resection is essential for accurate diagnosis.

ideal_answer: Ras is a family of related proteins expressed in virtually all animal cell types and tissues. Members of the Ras protein family belong to the class of small GTPases and play a central role in intracellular signal transduction. Ras is the prototypical member of the Ras superfamily, whose proteins share structural similarities and regulate a wide range of cellular processes. When Ras is activated ("switched on") in response to upstream signals, it in turn activates downstream effector proteins, ultimately leading to the regulation of genes involved in cell growth, differentiation, and survival. Mutations in Ras genes can result in constitutively active Ras proteins, causing persistent and unregulated signaling even in the absence of external stimuli. Ras functions as a key component of the ERK signaling pathway (RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK), a hierarchical kinase cascade initiated at the cell membrane by receptors for mitogens or growth factors. Upon activation, these receptors recruit adaptor proteins and guanine nucleotide exchange factors, which facilitate the activation of the small GTPase Ras by promoting its GTP-bound state. Active Ras (Ras-GTP) directly interacts with and activates Raf, a serine/threonine kinase also known as MAP kinase kinase kinase (MAPKKK). Raf subsequently phosphorylates and activates MEK (MAP kinase/ERK kinase), which in turn phosphorylates ERK1 and ERK2. Activated ERK translocates to the nucleus, where it regulates transcription factors and alters gene expression, thereby promoting processes such as cell growth, differentiation, and mitosis. In summary, active Ras (Ras-GTP) directly activates Raf kinase, initiating the MAPK signaling cascade.

questions.body: Which mutations in the Ras gene family are most commonly found in cancer?
ideal_answer: Ras is a family of related proteins expressed in virtually all animal cell types and tissues. Members of the Ras protein family belong to the class of small GTPases and play a central role in intracellular signal transduction. Ras is the prototypical member of the Ras superfamily, whose proteins share structural similarities and regulate a wide range of cellular processes. When Ras is activated ("switched on") in response to upstream signals, it activates downstream effector proteins, ultimately regulating genes involved in cell growth, differentiation, and survival. Mutations in Ras genes can lead to constitutively active Ras proteins, resulting in persistent and unregulated signaling even in the absence of external stimuli. Because these signaling pathways promote cell proliferation and survival, aberrant Ras activation is strongly associated with oncogenesis. The three Ras genes in humans, HRAS, KRAS, and NRAS, are among the most frequently mutated oncogenes in human cancers. Although mutations occur in all three, KRAS is the most commonly mutated isoform across many cancer types. These mutations often affect specific codons, particularly codon 12, and lead to impaired GTP hydrolysis, thereby locking Ras in its active (GTP-bound) state. Among the most common mutations is G12D, in which glycine is substituted by aspartic acid. This mutation reduces GTPase activity and promotes sustained activation of downstream signaling pathways, including the MAPK/ERK and PI3K/AKT pathways, contributing to uncontrolled cell proliferation and, in some cases, an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. The G12V mutation, involving substitution of glycine with valine at codon 12, similarly results in a constitutively active Ras protein with impaired GTP hydrolysis. Another frequent mutation, G12C, involves substitution of glycine with cysteine at codon 12 and leads to prolonged activation of Ras, as the protein exhibits reduced ability to transition back to its inactive GDP-bound state.

The most commonly found mutations in the Ras gene family in cancer are primarily substitutions at codon 12 of the KRAS gene, including KRAS G12D, KRAS G12V, and KRAS G12C. KRAS G12D is frequently observed in pancreatic, colorectal, and gastric cancers. KRAS G12V is predominant in uterine cancer and is also common in lung adenocarcinoma. KRAS G12C is most frequent in lung cancer. Less common but still notable variants include KRAS G13D and Q61 substitutions (such as Q61R/H), which can occur across Ras isoforms.
Mutations in KRAS, particularly at codon 12, are most commonly found in cancer. Common cancer-associated KRAS variants include G12D, G12V, and G12C.

Studies have identified KRAS mutations as frequent in adenocarcinomas of colon, lungs, and pancreas, driving carcinogenesis by altering cell signalling and reprogramming metabolism. Mutations in KRAS, particularly at codon 12, are common, with G12D being most common in pancreatic, colorectal, and gastric cancers, while G12V is predominant in uterine cancer, and G12C is most frequent in lung cancer. Analysis of 10,820 tumor samples found KRAS mutations in 19.97% of cases, with pancreatic cancer showing highest prevalence at 73.51%, followed by colorectal at 41.45%, uterine at 21.23%, and lung cancer at 11.24%. KRAS G12D, G12V, and G12C are most commonly found in cancer, with G12D being most frequent abnormality, followed by G12V and Q61R in some cohorts, such as one cohort where KRAS gene mutations were detected in 51.4% of cases.

The most common Ras gene family mutations in cancer are heterozygous substitutions in KRAS at codon 12, particularly G12D, G12V, and G12C. Additional recurrent hotspots include codon 13 (e.g., G13D) and codon 61 (e.g., Q61R), with Q61 mutations more frequent in NRAS and HRAS.

KRAS is the most common target, particularly in pancreatic, colorectal, and lung cancers. Mutations typically occur as point mutations at codons 12, 13, or 61. Among these, the G12D, G12V, and G12C variants are the most prevalent. Specifically, KRAS G12D is the most frequent mutation in pancreatic and colorectal cancers, while KRAS G12C is the predominant variant in lung cancer. KRAS G12V is also common, especially in uterine and lung adenocarcinomas. While KRAS is the most frequent overall, NRAS mutations are more common in myeloid malignancies, and HRAS mutations are relatively rare. questions.body: What effect does heroin have on the production of endorphins in humans?
ideal_answer: Heroin is an opioid drug that exerts its effects by binding to opioid receptors, which normally interact with endogenous ligands such as endorphins and enkephalins, forming a widespread and complex signaling network throughout the central and peripheral nervous systems. The opioid receptor family comprises three main classes: μ-, δ-, and κ-receptors. These receptors respond to exogenous opioid compounds, such as morphine and heroin, as well as to endogenous peptide ligands. Heroin primarily acts on μ-opioid receptors, leading to their overstimulation. This excessive activation triggers compensatory mechanisms within the brain, including a reduction in the endogenous production of endorphins. This effect is mediated by negative feedback processes, whereby prolonged receptor activation signals the system to downregulate endogenous opioid synthesis and release. As a result, chronic heroin use leads to decreased natural endorphin production and dependence on the drug to maintain normal physiological function. This neuroadaptation contributes to tolerance, withdrawal symptoms, and the reinforcing cycle of addiction.

Heroin, acting as an opioid receptor agonist, suppresses endogenous endorphin production through negative feedback mechanisms. Chronic use decreases beta-endorphin levels in the central nervous system and amniotic fluid, though plasma levels remain comparable to controls, suggesting compartment-specific suppression leading to dependence and withdrawal symptoms.

Heroin suppresses the production and release of endogenous endorphins, particularly beta-endorphin, in humans. As a potent exogenous mu-opioid receptor agonist, chronic heroin exposure triggers negative feedback inhibition on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. This neuroendocrine mechanism downregulates corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) secretion and reduces the processing of pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), thereby decreasing endogenous endorphin synthesis. Clinical and pharmacological evidence consistently demonstrates that short-acting opioid agonists like heroin depress baseline beta-endorphin levels. Furthermore, individuals with heroin addiction exhibit significantly reduced endorphin concentrations in bodily fluids and display blunted or absent endorphin responses to physiological stressors, such as hyperthermia, as well as impaired noradrenergic stimulation of POMC-related peptide release. Although some radioreceptor assays have reported elevated endorphin levels in dependent subjects, these findings are widely attributed to assay cross-reactivity with exogenous opioids or their metabolites rather than genuine upregulation of endogenous production. Consequently, chronic heroin use leads to a pronounced homeostatic downregulation and functional suppression of the endogenous endorphin system.

Heroin, an opioid drug, impacts the production of endorphins in humans by altering the brain's natural opioid systems. Here is a structured summary of its effects:

1. **Mechanism of Action**: Heroin binds to opioid receptors in the brain, mimicking the effects of endorphins but with greater potency. This can lead to a reduction in the body's own production of endorphins as the brain may perceive less need for them due to the external opioid influence.

2. **Chronic Use Effects**: Studies suggest that chronic heroin use can decrease the biosynthesis of endogenous opioid peptides, which are precursors to endorphins. This results in lower natural endorphin levels over time.

3. **Tolerance Development**: Prolonged heroin use often leads to tolerance, where higher doses are required to achieve the same effects. This is linked to changes in the brain's response to opioids and may involve reduced sensitivity to both the drug and naturally occurring endorphins.

4. **Withdrawal Symptoms**: When heroin use ceases, individuals may experience increased pain sensitivity, likely due to diminished endorphin levels. This underscores the dependency on external opioids for maintaining a sense of well-being and pain relief.

In conclusion, heroin disrupts the natural production of endorphins, leading to decreased levels over time. This disruption contributes to addiction dynamics and complicates the process of quitting the drug.

Heroin significantly suppresses the natural production of endorphins in humans through negative feedback regulation. When heroin binds to opioid receptors in the brain, it activates the same pathways as endogenous endorphins, leading the brain to reduce its own endorphin production to maintain balance. Chronic heroin use disrupts the body's natural opioid peptide systems, including beta-endorphin production, and suppresses endogenous opioid peptides, contributing to tolerance and dependence. Opioid use also disrupts normal circadian patterns that regulate endorphin production, further compromising the body's natural opioid systems. Studies indicate that with proper treatment, such as methadone maintenance therapy, beta-endorphin levels can potentially normalize over time, suggesting that the suppression of endorphin production may be reversible with sustained abstinence and medical intervention. Heroin interferes with complex biosynthetic pathways and receptor signaling involved in endorphin production, and this suppression is a key factor in opioid dependence, withdrawal symptoms, and the challenges of recovery from heroin addiction.

Heroin suppresses the endogenous production of endorphins in humans. When heroin enters the body, it is rapidly converted to morphine, which binds to mu-opioid receptors with high affinity. This exogenous activation of opioid receptors triggers a negative feedback mechanism in which the brain reduces its own synthesis and release of endogenous opioid peptides, including beta-endorphin, enkephalins, and dynorphins. Over time, with repeated heroin use, the brain downregulates opioid receptor density and decreases endogenous opioid production because the receptors are chronically stimulated by the drug. This neuroadaptation underlies physical dependence: when heroin is withdrawn, the suppressed endogenous opioid system is unable to compensate adequately, resulting in a deficit of normal opioid signaling. The consequence is a hypersensitive pain response, dysphoria, anxiety, and the classic withdrawal syndrome. The reduction in endorphin production also contributes to anhedonia during and after cessation of heroin use, as the natural reward system becomes blunted and dependent on exogenous opioids to function normally. Recovery of the endogenous opioid system can take weeks to months following abstinence.

Heroin disrupts the body's natural endorphin production through several mechanisms. It competes with natural endorphins for opioid receptor binding sites, as heroin and its metabolites bind to the same receptors (mu, delta, and kappa) that endogenous endorphins activate. Chronic heroin use triggers negative feedback mechanisms that suppress the body's production of endogenous opioids, including beta-endorphin and enkephalins, because the brain reduces its own opioid production when exposed to external opioids. Research indicates that heroin addiction is associated with profound dysregulation of the endogenous opioid system, leading to comprehensive disruption of natural endorphin function. Clinically, this results in tolerance (requiring more heroin for the same effect), withdrawal symptoms when heroin use stops (due to suppressed endorphin production), and long-term dependence as endogenous opioid production remains downregulated. However, while these pharmacological mechanisms are well-established, there is a lack of specific quantitative studies measuring changes in endorphin levels in humans following heroin use, and more clinical research is needed for precise measurements of endorphin suppression and recovery.

Heroin, an opioid drug, impacts the production of endorphins in humans by mimicking their effects but being significantly more potent. Chronic use of heroin can interfere with the body's natural production of endorphins, as the brain may reduce its own synthesis due to the presence of the drug providing similar euphoric and pain-relieving effects. This interference can lead to changes in the brain's chemistry, potentially resulting in decreased endorphin levels over time.

Research indicates that chronic opioid use alters the biosynthesis of endogenous opioid peptides, including endorphins, in specific brain regions. The downregulation or upregulation of opioid receptors due to heroin's presence might further contribute to this effect. Withdrawal symptoms, such as anxiety and increased pain sensitivity, suggest a disruption in the body's ability to maintain normal endorphin levels after prolonged use.

In summary, while acute use may not significantly affect endorphin production, chronic heroin use likely reduces the body's natural endorphin output, leading to changes in pain perception and reward mechanisms.

Heroin suppresses the body’s own endorphin activity and production rather than increasing it. Evidence shows that short-acting opioid agonists like heroin acutely lower circulating beta-endorphin levels in humans. Textbook sources describe repeated heroin use as causing downregulation of endogenous opioid production, resulting in decreased presynaptic endorphin production over time. This suppression contributes to withdrawal symptoms when the drug is stopped. Human studies report that beta-endorphin levels are depressed by heroin and morphine, while opioid antagonists such as naloxone elevate these levels. In heroin addicts during abstinence, beta-endorphin levels remain abnormal and decreased, indicating disruption of the endogenous opioid system. Chronic heroin use leads to lower beta-endorphin in opioid-dependent individuals compared to drug-naive controls, though findings are not entirely consistent across all addiction states. Repeated heroin exposure creates a relative deficiency in endogenous endorphin production, which is linked to withdrawal and tolerance. Long-term heroin use may lead to a lasting deficiency in the beta-endorphin system. The evidence is strongest for suppression or disruption of beta-endorphin levels and endogenous opioid function, with heroin acutely lowering these levels and repeated use associated with ongoing downregulation or deficiency of the endogenous system in humans.

Heroin suppresses or dysregulates the body’s endorphin system rather than increasing normal endogenous endorphin production. In humans, chronic heroin or opioid use is associated with blunted β-endorphin responses to stress, lower cerebrospinal fluid β-endorphin levels in opioid-dependent states, and disruption of endogenous opioid function. Studies show heroin addicts lack normal pituitary β-endorphin and ACTH responses to stress, indicating disrupted opioid reactivity. Opioid-dependent individuals have lower CSF β-endorphin during methadone maintenance and drug-free states compared to controls, although other endorphin-related measurements can sometimes be elevated, suggesting overall dysregulation. Reviews describe chronic heroin exposure as causing disruption of several endogenous opioid system components, including altered stress responsivity and persistent neurochemical changes. Repeated heroin use leads to downregulation of presynaptic endorphin production, resulting in deficiency after heroin is metabolized and contributing to withdrawal; recovery of endorphin production can take weeks. The human literature indicates dysregulation and functional suppression of normal endogenous opioid responses, not a straightforward universal decrease in every assay, as some measurements of endorphin activity may be elevated while β-endorphin is reduced.

questions.body: Are transposable elements found exclusively in nuclear DNA?
ideal_answer: Transposable elements (TEs), also known as "jumping genes", are DNA sequences capable of moving from one location in the genome to another. They play a significant role in shaping eukaryotic genomes by contributing to genome structure, evolution, and variability. While a substantial body of research has focused on the abundance and function of TEs in nuclear genomes, their presence in mitochondrial genomes remains relatively understudied. The occurrence of transposable elements in mitochondrial DNA is rare and not commonly observed across most organisms. However, such elements have been identified in certain fungi, including yeast, as well as in organisms such as Podospora anserina and Porphyridium. Although uncommon in nature, these findings demonstrate that transposable elements are not exclusively restricted to nuclear DNA.

questions.body: Does X-chromosome inactivation occur in males?
ideal_answer: X-chromosome inactivation is an essential mechanism for dosage compensation of X-linked genes between males and females and is established during the early stages of development in female cells. In normal males, X-chromosome inactivation does not occur because dosage compensation is unnecessary, as males possess only one X chromosome. However, cases of X-chromosome inactivation have been reported in males with abnormal numbers of sex chromosomes. These cases occur in conditions such as Klinefelter syndrome and other aneuploidies that result in multiple X chromosomes in male individuals. For example, individuals with Klinefelter syndrome typically have two X chromosomes and one Y chromosome (47,XXY). As a result, one of the X chromosomes undergoes inactivation in order to maintain dosage compensation, but only in this pathogenic situation and not in normal male, so the answer is no.

X-chromosome inactivation (XCI) typically does not occur in healthy XY males because they possess only one X chromosome. However, XCI does occur in males with supernumerary X chromosomes, such as those with Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY or 48,XXYY), to provide dosage compensation for the extra X-linked genes. In these individuals, the additional X chromosome is epigenetically silenced, though some genes may escape this inactivation.

Beyond chromosomal abnormalities, Xist, the noncoding RNA that mediates XCI, is transiently expressed in both males and females during early embryonic development at the onset of naive epiblast differentiation. Furthermore, XCI can be somatically activated in certain male human cancers, where the female-specific program of inactivation is accessed, leading to gene silencing and increased DNA methylation across the X chromosome. Experimental genetic modifications or the introduction of an X-inactivation center can also induce X-chromosome inactivation in male cells.

X-chromosome inactivation occurs in males under specific biological and pathological conditions. In normal 46,XY males, a process known as meiotic sex chromosome inactivation (MSCI) silences the X and Y chromosomes during the pachytene stage of spermatogenesis. In males with supernumerary X chromosomes, such as those with Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) or 49,XXXXY, X-chromosome inactivation occurs to compensate for the extra gene dosage, similar to the process in females. Additionally, X-chromosome inactivation is observed in XX males and can be somatically activated in certain male cancers through the expression of XIST, leading to gene silencing and increased DNA methylation across the X chromosome.

X-chromosome inactivation (XCI) generally does not occur in healthy XY males because they possess only one X chromosome. However, XCI does occur in males under several specific conditions. In individuals with Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY or 48,XXYY), who have supernumerary X chromosomes, XCI occurs to provide dosage compensation, similar to the process in females. Research also shows that XCI can be somatically activated in certain male human cancers across diverse lineages, where the XIST gene is expressed and leads to gene silencing and increased DNA methylation on the X chromosome. Furthermore, Xist is transiently expressed in male embryos at the onset of differentiation, and XCI is present in male germ cells. Experimental models have also demonstrated that ectopic XCI can be induced in male cells through genetic mutations or the introduction of a human X inactivation center.

No, X-chromosome inactivation does not occur in males under normal circumstances. Males have only one X chromosome, so there is no need for X-inactivation as a dosage compensation mechanism. X-inactivation evolved specifically for individuals with multiple X chromosomes, primarily XX females. However, X-inactivation does occur in males with chromosomal abnormalities, such as Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) and other XXY variants, where studies confirm evidence of X-chromosome inactivation to achieve dosage compensation. Additionally, a distinct process called meiotic sex chromosome inactivation occurs in normal male germ cells during spermatogenesis, which is a temporary silencing mechanism during meiosis and affects both X and Y chromosomes in the male germline, but is different from the permanent X-inactivation in somatic cells.

No, X-chromosome inactivation (XCI) does not occur in males under normal circumstances. XCI is a dosage compensation mechanism in female mammals (XX) that transcriptionally silences one of the two X chromosomes in each somatic cell, ensuring that X-linked gene expression is roughly equivalent between females and males. Males have only one X chromosome (XY), so there is no need for inactivation, and that single X chromosome remains active. The Y chromosome is not subject to XCI. However, there is an important exception: during male meiosis, the X and Y chromosomes undergo meiotic sex chromosome inactivation (MSCI) in the pachytene stage of spermatogenesis, where both sex chromosomes are transcriptionally silenced within the sex body. This is a distinct process from somatic XCI and is confined to germ cells. Additionally, males with Klinefelter syndrome (XXY) do undergo XCI, silencing one X chromosome, similar to normal females, since the presence of two X chromosomes triggers the inactivation machinery regardless of the presence of a Y chromosome.

No, X-chromosome inactivation does not occur in typical males. Normal males have an XY chromosome configuration with only one X chromosome, so classical X-inactivation is unnecessary. Molecular evidence shows that XIST expression, which is associated with X-inactivation, is minimal to absent in normal XY males, indicating no active X-inactivation process. There is a distinct process called meiotic sex chromosome inactivation (MSCI) during male spermatogenesis, but this is different from classical X-inactivation. In males with extra X chromosomes, such as those with Klinefelter syndrome (XXY), there is evidence of skewed X-chromosome inactivation to compensate for the extra X. Classical X-chromosome inactivation is a mechanism for XX females to balance X-linked gene expression, and normal XY males do not require or undergo this process.

In normal male (XY) somatic tissues, X‑chromosome inactivation is generally absent because males have only one X chromosome and dosage compensation is achieved by having that single active X. However, XCI can occur in specific male contexts: it is reported in germ cells, in individuals with supernumerary X chromosomes (e.g., XXY or XX males), and can be experimentally initiated in male embryonic stem cells; hallmarks of XCI have also been observed in some male cancers. Thus, while XCI is not a typical feature of normal male somatic cells, it can occur in males under particular biological or pathological conditions.

Glioblastomas (GBM), the most common primary brain tumors, infiltrate the brain, grow rapidly, and are refractory to current therapies. Signature genetic lesions in glioblastomas include mutation of the epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase (EGFR) receptor tyrosine kinase and activating mutations in components of the PI-3 kinase (PI3K) pathway. Despite years of study, how these pathways specifically regulate glial pathogenesis is unclear. To address the genetic and cellular origins of this disease, a novel Drosophila GBM model has been developed in which glial progenitor cells give rise to proliferative and invasive neoplastic cells that create transplantable tumors in response to constitutive co-activation of the EGFR-Ras and PI3K pathways.

questions.body: For which types of cancer have Drosophila melanogaster models ("fly avatars") been generated?
ideal_answer: Cancer is a complex disease in which multiple factors - including genetic aberrations, epigenetic modifications, metabolic reprogramming, and the tumor microenvironment - contribute to tumor development and progression. In the traditional anticancer drug discovery pipeline, candidate compounds are typically screened in vitro using two-dimensional or three-dimensional cell culture systems. The evolutionary conservation of key biological pathways between the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster and humans, along with its reduced genetic redundancy, has long established Drosophila as a valuable genetic model organism. The common fruit fly has therefore emerged as an effective system for modeling human cancers. Moreover, Drosophila has opened new avenues for personalized cancer therapy. So-called "fly avatars", engineered to carry the same mutations as an individual patient, are used to screen multiple therapeutic agents targeting different pathways in order to identify the most effective drug combinations. Numerous studies have successfully generated Drosophila models of colorectal, lung, thyroid, and brain cancers. These models have been employed in high-throughput screening of FDA-approved drugs, leading to the identification of compounds capable of reducing tumor cell proliferation and rescuing disease-related phenotypes. Additionally, such approaches have been applied in patients with adenoid cystic carcinoma, demonstrating the translational potential of this model. In summary, Drosophila avatars represent a modern and promising strategy for identifying personalized anticancer therapies tailored to individual patients, rather than relying solely on generalized treatment approaches.

questions.body: What are the common symptoms of Cushing's Syndrome?
ideal_answer: Discriminatory features of Cushing Syndrome (CS) include truncal obesity (i.e., abdominal weight gain), round reddish "moon" face, buffalo hump (i.e, dorsocervical fat pad), supraclavicular (i.e., above the collarbone) fullness, and thinning extremities. CS patients also often exhibit proximal muscle weakness, hypertension, osteoporosis/osteopenia and a history of (unexplained) fractures, reddish purple striae, bruising with no obvious trauma, skin thinning, poor wound healing, and acne. Particularly women patients exhibit menstrual irregularity, female balding, and hirsutism (extra growth of dark or coarse hair in men-like areas like the face, chest, and back). Key psychological and psychiatric symptoms include sleeping disorders, anxiety, depression, cognitive dysfunction (i.e., memory/concentration issues), and loss of libido.

The common symptoms of Cushing's Syndrome can be categorized into highly specific features, common but non-specific features, and associated manifestations or complications. Highly specific features include wide purple striae, proximal muscle weakness or myopathy, characteristic fat redistribution (truncal obesity, supraclavicular fat deposition, moon facies), facial plethora, easy bruising or thin fragile skin, and in children, growth retardation combined with weight gain. Common but non-specific features, which are also prevalent in the general population, include generalized or central weight gain and obesity, hypertension, hyperglycemia or diabetes, hirsutism, acne, neurocognitive changes, mood disorders or depression, and reproductive abnormalities such as menstrual irregularities or impotence. Associated manifestations and downstream morbidities or complications resulting from chronic hypercortisolism include protein catabolism, immunosuppression with increased infection risk, osteoporosis or fragility fractures, and cardiovascular or thromboembolic disease.

Cushing's syndrome presents with a combination of distinctive glucocorticoid-excess signs and overlapping systemic manifestations. Classical features include central or truncal obesity, weight gain, proximal muscle weakness, wide purple striae, facial plethora, easy bruising (ecchymoses), and characteristic fat deposition in the supraclavicular and supraorbital regions. Metabolic and systemic symptoms commonly involve hypertension, hyperglycemia (diabetes mellitus), hypokalemia, and unexplained osteoporosis. Patients also frequently experience reproductive abnormalities (such as menstrual irregularities and impotence), depression, mood disorders, and neurocognitive changes. Dermatological signs like hirsutism and acne are common, while children may present with growth retardation. Chronic hypercortisolism further predisposes individuals to comorbidities such as cardiovascular disease, thromboembolic events, and increased susceptibility to infections.

Unexpectedly, respiration in INS-1E insulinoma cells and primary human islets was unaltered in the presence of chloramphenicol. Resting respiratory rates and glucose stimulated acceleration of respiration were also not lowered when a range of antibiotics including, thiamphenicol, streptomycin, gentamycin and doxycycline known to interfere with bacterial protein synthesis were tested. ideal_answer: Cortisol secretion is regulated by the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. It involves a hormonal cascade where the hypothalamus releases the corticotropin releasing hormone (CRH), which signals the release of the adrenocorticotropin releasing hormone (ACTH) by the pituitary, which in turn stimulates the production of cortisol in the adrenal cortex and its release into circulation. As a result, ROS are considered one of the most cytotoxic endogenous factors in cells. However, their production is still necessary because they can have beneficial effects when their concentration is properly regulated.

The local microenvironment, or niche, of a cancer cell plays important roles in cancer development. A major component of the niche is the extracellular matrix (ECM), a complex network of macromolecules with distinctive physical, biochemical, and biomechanical properties. Although tightly controlled during embryonic development and organ homeostasis, the ECM is commonly deregulated and becomes disorganized in diseases such as cancer. Abnormal ECM affects cancer progression by directly promoting cellular transformation and metastasis. Importantly, however, ECM anomalies also deregulate behavior of stromal cells, facilitate tumor-associated angiogenesis and inflammation, and thus lead to generation of a tumorigenic microenvironment. Understanding how ECM composition and topography are maintained and how their deregulation influences cancer progression may help develop new therapeutic interventions by targeting the tumor niche.

Cancer progression is a multistep process during which normal cells exhibit molecular changes that culminate into the highly malignant and metastatic phenotype, observed in cancerous tissues. The initiation of cell transformation is generally associated with genetic alterations in normal cells that lead to the loss of intercellular- and/or extracellular-matrix- (ECM-) mediated cell adhesion. Transformed cells undergo rapid multiplication and generate more modifications in adhesion and motility-related molecules which allow them to escape from the original site and acquire invasive characteristics. Integrins, which are multifunctional adhesion receptors, and are present, on normal as well as transformed cells, assist the cells undergoing tumor progression in creating the appropriate environment for their survival, growth, and invasion. In this paper, we have briefly discussed the role of ECM proteins and integrins during cancer progression and described some unique conditions where adhesion-related changes could induce genetic mutations in anchorage-independent tumor model systems.

The composition of the extracellular matrix in tumors is vastly different from that found in the normal tissue counterparts. As the extracellular matrix can signal to cells via integrin binding and activation, which is known to modulate cell proliferation, survival and migration, it may influence the response of both tumor and endothelial cells to anticancer therapies. Certain tumor-associated extracellular matrix proteins have been shown to confer resistance to chemotherapeutic drugs, radiation and anti-angiogenic factors. The current literature regarding this phenomenon and the potential therapeutic modalities to overcome extracellular matrix-induced resistance will be discussed.

Almost three decades ago, we presented a model where the extracellular matrix (ECM) was postulated to influence gene expression and tissue-specificity through the action of ECM receptors and the cytoskeleton. This hypothesis implied that ECM molecules could signal to the nucleus and that the unit of function in higher organisms was not the cell alone, but the cell plus its microenvironment. We now know that ECM invokes changes in tissue and organ architecture and that tissue, cell, nuclear, and chromatin structure are changed profoundly as a result of and during malignant progression. Whereas some evidence has been generated for a link between ECM-induced alterations in tissue architecture and changes in both nuclear and chromatin organization, the manner by which these changes actively induce or repress gene expression in normal and malignant cells is a topic in need of further attention. Here, we will discuss some key findings that may provide insights into mechanisms through which ECM could influence gene transcription and how tumor cells acquire the ability to overcome these levels of control.

The sites of interaction between a cell and its surrounding microenvironment serve as dynamic signaling hubs that regulate cellular adaptations during developmental processes, immune functions, wound healing, cell migration, cancer invasion and metastasis, as well as in many other disease states. For most cell types, these interactions are established by integrin receptors binding directly to extracellular matrix proteins, such as the numerous collagens or fibronectin. questions.body: Can the extracellular matrix influence the transformation of normal cells into cancer cells?
ideal_answer: The extracellular matrix (ECM) can significantly influence the transformation of normal cells into cancerous cells, as it regulates key signaling pathways involved in cell growth, survival, differentiation, and tissue organization. This regulation is mediated by a variety of ECM components, associated proteins, and inflammatory mediators, as well as specific interactions between cells and the ECM. Alterations in ECM composition, structure, and stiffness can disrupt normal cellular signaling and promote a tumorigenic microenvironment. Excessive ECM deposition and remodeling, often referred to as fibrosis or desmoplasia, can contribute to tumor development and progression in surrounding tissues. Several ECM-related molecules are implicated in tumorigenesis. For example, matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP2) is involved in ECM degradation and can facilitate tumor invasion and metastasis. Galectin-3 plays roles in cell adhesion, apoptosis regulation, and immune modulation, and has been associated with cancer progression. Hyaluronan, a major ECM component, can influence cell proliferation, migration, and inflammation depending on its molecular weight and context. Overall, while ECM components are not inherently carcinogenic, their dysregulation can alter signaling pathways, promote proliferation, inhibit apoptosis, and contribute to malignant transformation.

Yes, the extracellular matrix (ECM) plays a significant role in influencing the transformation of normal cells into cancer cells. The ECM is not merely a passive scaffold but an active participant in cellular communication and regulation. Changes in the ECM, such as increased stiffness or altered composition due to factors like inflammation, fibrosis, or pollution, can create a microenvironment that promotes oncogenesis.

For instance, excessive ECM deposition, as seen in conditions like oral submucous fibrosis (OSF), can lead to tissue sclerosis and potentially facilitate cancer transformation. Pollutants inducing ECM accumulation during liver fibrosis may set the stage for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Proteins such as galectin-3 and enzymes like MMP2 are involved in ECM remodeling, influencing tumor progression and metastasis.

Additionally, ECM components like hyaluronan (HA) interact with receptors to accelerate cancer cell invasion. Inflammatory bowel diseases linked to colon cancer involve ECM alterations that promote transformation through signaling pathways affecting epithelial cells. Thus, the ECM's dynamic interactions significantly contribute to creating a pro-cancerous environment, underscoring its critical role in cancer development.

The extracellular matrix (ECM) can influence the transformation of normal cells into cancer cells. Evidence shows ECM accumulation in fibrotic diseases (e.g., oral submucous fibrosis, liver fibrosis) is directly linked to cancer transformation, while ECM-induced signaling (e.g., integrin or CD168 pathways) in non-transformed cells promotes pro-oncogenic behaviors like COX-2 upregulation, ROS generation, and cell migration. Additionally, ECM components (e.g., hyaluronan, galectin-3) and remodeling enzymes (e.g., MMP2) actively contribute to oncogenic signaling and progression.

Yes, the extracellular matrix (ECM) significantly influences the transformation of normal cells into cancer cells. Abnormalities in the interactions between cells and the ECM are considered a hallmark of malignant transformation. Alterations in the stromal microenvironment, including changes in ECM composition, structure, and architecture, can be both necessary and sufficient to induce malignant behavior even in genetically normal cells. 

These modifications can trigger specific signal transduction pathways and oncogene-mediated cell reprogramming, leading to the loss of cell adhesion, increased proliferation, and invasion. For example, inflammation-induced modulations of the ECM can promote cancer transformation in tissues like the intestinal epithelium. Furthermore, the ECM acts as a reservoir for growth factors and signaling molecules that regulate tissue homeostasis; when this regulation is disrupted or the ECM becomes disorganized, it can drive the progressive transformation of normal cells into highly malignant ones. Thus, the ECM is a critical epigenetic modifier of cell behavior and a key driver of tumorigenesis.

Yes. The extracellular matrix can strongly influence whether normal cells acquire cancer-like properties. Changes in ECM composition, stiffness, adhesion signaling, and cell-ECM interactions can alter signal transduction, mechanotransduction, gene expression, survival, proliferation, invasion, and genomic stability. Loss or abnormal remodeling of ECM-mediated adhesion is linked to malignant transformation, and increased ECM rigidity can cooperate with oncogenic signals to reprogram normal cells into tumor-initiating cells. Inflammatory ECM changes can also promote transformation. However, the ECM usually acts together with oncogenic, inflammatory, or microenvironmental signals rather than as the only cause.

Yes, the extracellular matrix (ECM) significantly influences the transformation of normal cells into cancer cells. The ECM is not merely a structural scaffold but a dynamic component of the tumor microenvironment that regulates essential cellular functions. Changes in the biophysical properties of the ECM, particularly increased stiffness and rigidity, can directly drive oncogenic transformation and the development of malignant phenotypes. This occurs through aberrant mechanotransduction, where physical forces from a stiffened matrix trigger intracellular signaling pathways, such as Akt signaling, and promote the assembly of focal adhesions. Additionally, biochemical alterations and epigenetic deregulation of cell-matrix interactions can disrupt homeostatic control of tissue architecture, cell proliferation, and survival. These modifications in the ECM density and composition act as critical drivers for tumor initiation, progression, and metastasis.

Yes, the extracellular matrix (ECM) can influence the transformation of normal cells into cancer cells. Research shows that ECM stiffness and mechanotransduction pathways directly affect cancer development and malignant transformation by regulating tissue integrity and cellular behavior. Protein interaction analyses demonstrate direct molecular connections between ECM components such as collagen, fibronectin, laminin, and integrins, and key oncogenic proteins including TP53, MYC, EGFR, KRAS, and PIK3CA, with numerous documented protein-protein interactions. Multiple ECM-mediated signaling routes promote cellular transformation, including integrin-mediated focal adhesion signaling, FAK and SRC kinase activation, YAP/TAZ mechanotransduction, TGF-β/SMAD signaling leading to epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and matrix metalloproteinase remodeling pathways. Specific ECM proteins and remodeling enzymes like MMPs and lysyl oxidase play roles in transformation processes, and studies have documented ECM targeting as a therapeutic strategy, confirming its involvement in cancer progression. Overall, ECM modifications generate biochemical and biophysical signals that can directly trigger oncogenic pathways, making the extracellular matrix a critical factor in the transformation of normal cells to malignancy.

Yes, the extracellular matrix (ECM) can significantly influence the transformation of normal cells into cancer cells. The ECM provides not only structural support but also biochemical and mechanical signals that regulate cell proliferation, survival, differentiation, and migration. Alterations in ECM composition, stiffness, and remodeling can promote malignant transformation. For example, increased matrix stiffness, driven by collagen crosslinking via lysyl oxidase, activates integrin signaling and downstream pathways such as PI3K/AKT and RAS/MAPK, which can override normal growth controls. ECM components like fibronectin, laminin, and various collagens interact with cell surface receptors, modulating gene expression and epigenetic states that favor a transformed phenotype. Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), which remodel the ECM, release sequestered growth factors such as TGF-β, EGF, and VEGF, further driving oncogenic signaling. Additionally, a fibrotic or dysregulated ECM microenvironment can impair normal epithelial polarity and disrupt tissue architecture, lowering the threshold for malignant transformation. Studies using 3D culture models have demonstrated that restoring normal ECM context can revert certain cancer cell behaviors, underscoring the ECM's active role in both initiating and maintaining the transformed state.

Yes, the extracellular matrix (ECM) can influence the transformation of normal cells into cancer cells. Research data shows extensive protein-protein interactions between ECM components such as fibronectin, integrins, collagen, and laminin with key oncogenic proteins including TP53, EGFR, MYC, PTEN, PIK3CA, and APC, indicating direct molecular crosstalk with cancer-related signaling pathways. Published studies have examined the mechanistic role of the ECM in cancer transformation, including matrix stiffness, mechanotransduction, ECM-mediated regulation of oncogenic signaling, integrin and focal adhesion kinase pathways, and anoikis resistance as a hallmark of cancer cells. Multiple biological pathways, such as integrin signaling, focal adhesion, TGF-beta, Wnt signaling, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition, link ECM signaling to transformation processes. Comprehensive evidence from protein interaction databases and literature strongly supports the ECM's role in influencing cellular transformation to cancer.

Yes, the extracellular matrix (ECM) can influence the transformation of normal cells into cancer cells. ideal_answer: Mitochondria are semi-autonomous organelles that contain their own DNA (mtDNA) and replicate independently of the nuclear genome. They play a crucial role in cellular processes such as energy production, metabolism, and signaling. Although mitochondrial inheritance is traditionally considered to be strictly maternal, rare exceptions have been reported in which paternal mitochondrial DNA is transmitted to the offspring. This phenomenon, known as paternal leakage, has been observed in clinical studies, including cases where individuals carry mtDNA of paternal origin, sometimes alongside maternal mtDNA (heteroplasmy). These findings indicate that paternal mtDNA can not only be inherited but, in rare instances, may contribute significantly to the overall mtDNA pool in an individual. Therefore, while mitochondrial inheritance is predominantly maternal, it is not exclusively so.

Cushing's disease (CD) is remarkably prevalent among females; however, more severe clinical presentation and adverse outcomes have been found in males. The purpose of this study was to investigate the overall clinical profile and biochemical parameters in patients with CD to identify the gender differences. Here we describe our series of CD patients referred to our medical center during 2012-2013. Among 73 cases, females presented a marked preponderance compared to males. Males had significantly higher ACTH, BMI, HbA1c, systolic blood pressure, and hemoglobin than females. For the first time, the incidence of fatty liver and hepatic function was also shown to be elevated in males. Multiple linear regression analysis was performed to further investigate the correlation of risk factors with hypokalemia, HbA1c, and systolic blood pressure. Gender and serum cortisol were associated with hypokalemia. Age, gender, and serum cortisol were significantly associated with HbA1c. Additionally, only gender was significantly associated with systolic blood pressure. Regarding clinical presentation, purple striae seemed to occur more frequently in males than in females. Thus, more severe clinical presentation, biochemical parameters, and complications were found in males than in females. Clinical professionals should pay more attention to the diagnosis and management of males with CD.
